In pasture, on lower slopes of Lismalanny Hill. Rectangular arrangement of four stones. North pair, 1.9m apart, have parallel axes aligned NNE-SSW. West stone is broken with upper portion lying against its base; it is 0.7m L, 0.2m T and was c. 1.6m H when intact. East stone is 0.55m L, 0.35m T and 1.5m H. Second pair, 7.5m to S, stand 1.8m apart with long axes more or less at right angles to opposing N counterparts. West stone is 0.8m L, 0.4m T and 1.9m H. East stone leans to S; it is 0.8m L, 0.5m T and 1.7m H. Windele, in the mid-19th-century (Grove White 1905-25, vol. 4, 3-4), records having seen five stones here and was informed that there had been eight. Exact nature of site uncertain. Early ecclesiastical enclosure (13887) 100m to NNW. (Ó Nualláin 1984b, 71, no. 7)

On low ridge in gently rolling pasture; named 'Acuthoge' on 1842 and 1905 OS 6-inch maps. Remains comprise large subcircular cairn (diam. c. 36m; max. H c. 1.5m) (CO024-056001-) with central chamber. Cairn was opened c. 1838 and its material quarried leaving hollowed out area in centre; cairn was then 5-6m in height. Exposed within hollow is open chamber (L 2.2m; Wth 1.5m; H 1.7m at W end, 1.4m at E end), aligned E-W, represented by single N and S sidestones with inset E backstone, and covered by single roofstone. Chamber decreases in height from W to E. Various traditions of objects and bones found with chamber but none are reliable. Structure is similar to wedge tomb but large covering mound is not typical of such monuments and could be secondary feature. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1982, 1, no. 1)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 4: North Cork' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2000). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload/revision: 14 January 2009

CO027-086----:
In pasture, on top of low gently sloping knoll c. 450m S of Funshion River. One of the largest wedge tombs in the country, it was excavated in 1934 (Leask and Price 1936). The remains comprise a long, subrectangular gallery, aligned WNW-ESE, divided into a W main chamber (L 6.2m, Wth c. 1.7m) and a small E end chamber (L c. 0.9m; Wth 1.2m); the whole is covered by three roofstones. The main chamber is 1.8m H at W and 1.2m at E end. Gallery walls are doubled and flanked on either side by massive outer-walling. Three buttress stones stand at the E end of the gallery. A line of low kerbstones to the S of the gallery, joining buttress stones at the E end, encloses the low remains of a cairn; some remains of a cairn were found to the N of the gallery but no kerb was located. The W end of the monument is very ruined and though the original design is unclear, a portico seems likely. On the floor of the end chamber were found the headless skeleton of a woman accompanied by burnt animal bones and a bone pin; this was probably the primary burial. Higher up were cremated human bones and some coarse pot sherds. Two inhumations, including three skulls, were found in the main chamber, with sherds of coarse pottery. An additional skull appeared to match the female skeleton from the end of the chamber. Evidence for other burials were found in the portico area including a probable cist containing inhumation and sherds of possible food vessel (CO027-169----). Three radiocarbon determinations indicate that the burials could have taken place within the shortest calibrated range of 2202-2138 BC (Brindley and Lanting 1991-92, 21). (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1982, 2-4, no. 3; Ó Riordáin and Waddell 1993, 94).
This is a National Monument in State Guardianship (no. 318).
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 4: North Cork' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2000). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload/revision: 14 January 2009

Situated on a bog-covered saddle of the NE fringe of the Derrynasaggart Mountains rising to Claragh Mountain to the NE and overlooking the Blackwater valley to the NW. The stone circle is incomplete: two upright stones stand 1.27m apart. The W stone (1.15m x 0.28m; H 0.7m) is a probable axial stone and the E stone (0.67m x 0.47m; H 0.7m) is a possible entrance stone. The measurement along the presumed axis, atypically aligned NNW-SSE, is 1.6m. The relationship of the circle to two slabs lying prostrate to S (1.95m) and SW (1.4m) is unclear, possibly they are displaced orthostats.

CO042-056001-:
On top of slight natural knoll in flat pasture, c. 120m N of Leapford Stream. There is a possible megalithic tomb (CO042-056002-) c. 60m to the SW, and a standing stone pair (CO042-057----) c. 350m to the NE. Excavation of this wedge tomb in 1957 (O'Kelly 1958a) revealed a gallery, aligned NE-SW (L 5.75m; Wth 1.2m at SW end, 0.75m at NE). A low sill and jamb-like slab separates the main chamber from the portico, immediately inside the SW end of which stands a low pillar stone. The gallery is surrounded by a U-shaped setting of outer-walling, doubled towards the SW, and joined to the gallery by a façade. The structure had been enveloped in an ovoid or D-shaped cairn (L 11.5m; Wth 9.7m), at the edge of which were a series of spaced sockets for probable kerb stones. Beyond the gallery entrance and façade were four further sockets and trench interpreted as kerb revetment for blocking material. Evidence for three cremated burials were found in the main chamber; in a shallow pit just NE of the sill, in a pit towards NE end, and in area between it and the gallery end. Three worked flints were recovered from primary levels within the main chamber. A small hearth was uncovered immediately N of the outer-walling. Three C14 determinations indicated a single phase of activity that occurred sometime within the calibrated range of 1412-1308 BC, with the most probable explanation suggesting that the gallery and the outer-wall were constructed sometime in the early Bronze Age and subsequently enhanced by a concentric kerb setting (Brindley and Lanting 1991-92, 20-21). (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1982, 5, no. 6)
This is a National Monument in State Guardianship (no. 502).
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 4: North Cork' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2000). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

On a gently sloping terrace on a S-facing slope in the foothills of the Boggeragh Mountains overlooking the valley of the Awboy River to the W and S. The remains consist of a gallery (L c. 4m; Wth 1.3m at W, 1.4m at centre and narrowing sharply at E to 0.5m), aligned NW-SE, represented by five sidestones to N and four to S; no backstone is visible. Two outer-wall stones stand to the N and S of the gallery. The S section of the gallery is covered by a roofstone (2.4m x 2m; T 0.2-0.25m) and a second displaced roofstone (2.05m x 0.9m; T 0.25m) lies at an angle at the W end of the gallery which is partly blocked with fill. Traces of a mound to the N, W and S appear to be the result of field clearance. Another wedge tomb (CO049-067----) is located 300m to the W.
The above description is derived from 'The Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 5' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009).
Date of upload: 22 December 2009

On a S-facing slope of the SE spur of Museramore Mountain. This wedge tomb consists of a gallery (min. L 4m; Wth 1.3m at W, narrowing to 0.8m towards the centre) aligned WNW-ESE. The S side of the gallery is represented by four stones. Only two stones of the N side remain; the stones forming its E end and the backstone are missing. Two longitudinally set jamb stones stand inside the W end narrowing the gallery entrance width to 0.65m. The E section of the gallery is covered by a single roofstone (2.2m x 2.3m; T 0.4m at W, narrowing to 0.3m at E). The gallery is surrounded by seven outer-wall stones which curve around its E end. A prostrate slab (1.7m x 0.55m; T c. 0.2m) lies immediately SE of the outer-walling; this may be a displaced roofstone. The tomb is known locally as the 'mass-rock'. Another wedge tomb (CO049-066----) is located 300m to the E.
The above description is derived from 'The Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 5' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009).
Date of upload: 22 December 2009

CO051-043001-:
In level pasture, on W side of Fiddler's Brook. Monument destroyed sometime prior to 1910. Pieces of pottery found in course of destruction. Early accounts record five-stone circle having internal measurement along main axis, apparently aligned N-S, of c. 3.3m. Orthostats were c. 0.9m to c. 1.8m L and c. 0.75m to c. 0.9m H. According to OS Memoranda for Co. Cork (1933), four of the stones were buried by the landowner in field where they stood; the fifth (CO051-043004-) was removed to the SE corner and used as gate pillar. This stone was shown on 1938 OS 6-inch map, named 'Gallán'; there is now no visible surface trace. A three-stone row (CO051-043003-) stood c. 75m to ENE. (RIA MS 12. W.2, no. 32; O Nualláin 1984a, 33, no. 58; Walsh 1998)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 3: Mid Cork' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Updated by: Paul Walsh
Revised date of upload: 20 April 2015

Second stone, standing in 1910, stood c. 2.4m to SW; it measured c. 1.1m L, c. 0.4m T and 2.4m H. Third stones stood c. 1.5m to SW; it measured c. 0.9m L and 1.2m H. OS records (1933) note that stones were removed twenty years previously to form gate pillars (CO051-043002-) to N; depicted on 1938 OS 6-inch map as pair of stones, next to or in fence, c. 30m to N; E gate pillar remains (H 1.2m; 0.75m x 0.25m). Five-stone circle (CO051-043001-) stood c. 75m to WSW. (RIA MS 12. W.2, no. 32; Condon 1916, 129, No. 105)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 3: Mid Cork' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

Single orthostat to S may be sidestone; second leaning orthostat to W may be facade stone. Structure incorporated in a low mound. CO058-075----:
Within a dense coniferous forest planted in the 1970s, on the upper SW-facing slopes of Knockacommeen. According to local information, when peat was cut in this general area in the 1960s a chamber was exposed consisting of a large roofstone resting on upright slabs. The structure collapsed in the late 1960s when the sidestones shifted inwards. A series of large displaced stones are visible at the site, including the possible roofstone (2.2m x 2m); these are largely concealed beneath forest clearance and debris. The description of the monument is indicative of a megalithic tomb, and given that two other wedge tombs occur on the mountain (CO058-060---- and especially CO058-076----, c. 500m and c. 1.1km, respectively to the ENE), this might be considered another example of this class.
The above description is derived from 'The Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 5' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009).
Date of upload: 22 December 2009
CO058-076----:
Remains of this tomb were exposed in the course of peat cutting on the upper S slopes of Knockacommeen Mountain. The S and E sides of the roofstone (2.5m x 1.6m; T 0.17m) and part of the S side are exposed in the cutaway bog face. It consists of a chamber (L 1.95; Wth 0.9m at W, narrowing slightly to 0.84m at E), aligned E-W. Both the N and S sides are formed by two slabs and the E end is closed by a backstone (H 0.30m). The roofstone rests on the sidestones, backstone and on a pad-stone on top of the W end of the S side. A possible outer-wall stone is exposed immediately S of the chamber, slightly set back from the W end. A second wedge tomb (CO058-060----) stands c. 700m to the WSW and the remains of a possible third (CO058-075----) are within the forest c. 1.1km to the WSW.
The above description is derived from 'The Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 5' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009).
Date of upload: 22 December 2009
CO058-077----:
This monument was reported to the Archaeological Survey of Ireland by Tony Miller on 28th January 2013. He describes it as follows: "This is a standing stone shown to me by the occupant of a nearby house. It is situated approximately 8 meters west of a small local road north of the village of Coolea. It is on the edge of a recently reclaimed field in amongst a stand of mature conifers. To the north and east are areas of extensive forestry. The land is south facing overlooking the river valley below, while behind it stretches up towards the county bounds. The stone itself is roughly rectangular in shape with a possible recent break on its eastern side. It is orientated NNE-SSW (20°-200°) and measures c. 0.95m high, c. 0.74 long and c. 0.55m in width."
Compiled by: Denis Power
Date of upload: 29 January 2013

CO059-187----:
On a gently sloping shoulder on a NE-facing slope in the foothills of the Boggeragh Mountains with fine views to the E over the valley of the Awboy River. The remains consist of a gallery (L 1.55m; Wth 0.9m at W, narrowing to 0.55m at E) aligned NW-SE, covered by a single roofstone (2.45m x 2.15m; T 0.35m). The gallery is represented by three sidestones to the N and three to the S with a transversely set jamb-like stone at its W end. The gallery is closed by a backstone at E. Two outer-wall stones to the N of the gallery lean markedly to the N and a large outer-wall stone is set 0.4m outside the backstone at E. A standing stone (CO059-025----) is located c. 140m to the WNW.
The above description is derived from 'The Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 5' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009).
Date of upload: 22 December 2009

CO062-130----:
On flat patch of ground, in rolling pasture, on N side of Shournagh River basin. One stone remains, long axis NE-SW; it is 2.2m L, 0.65m T and 3m H; second stone, standing in 1934, stood c. 2.6m to SW (O Nualláin 1988, 245, no. 99). According to local information, second stone fell during storm on Christmas Eve 1966. Twelve stones found in 'immediate locality' of stone pair, 'some much larger, lying on the ground partly buried in the boggy soil of the place' (Caulfield 1866, 293). Local tradition that there were at least 7 stones in this field.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 3: Mid Cork' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

CO069-090----:
Described by Colm Chambers as 'located at an altitude of 150—160m OD, on the south side of a large rock outcrop above the Sullane River, which flows about 500m to the north. The surrounding terrain is uncultivated, consisting of rocky outcrops with a patchy cover of gorse, grasses and boggy areas. There is a wide aspect to the south and south-west along with views of the Paps and Mullaghanish mountains to the north-west, north and north-east.
The monument is known locally as Follaig Na Gabhar, which translates as ‘the neglected place of the goat’ or ‘the hiding place of the goat’. A megalithic tomb (CO069-077----) was recorded in 1898 in the adjoining townlands of Rahoonagh East and Rahoonagh West as ‘… a large cromleac’ (Murphy, 1898, 15; Power el al., 1997, 9). However, the site has not been identified and the ‘cromleac’ described by Murphy may be the wedge tomb discussed here.
The tomb is aligned towards an unrecorded standing stone 25m to the south-south-west. The standing stone (CO069-091----) is about 1.5m tall, 0.6m wide at the base and tapers sharply at its top. Vertical lines of quartz stripe the stone. The long face of the standing stone is orientated in the direction of the wedge-tomb. A stone pair (CO069-020) stand 100m to the west of the tomb.
The monument’s long axis runs from the north-north-east to south-south-west and is 4.02m in length. It consists of a simple box-like chamber measuring 2m by 2m, the walls of which narrow towards the north-north-east. This chamber consists of a single upright slab on the south-south-west and east-south-east sides, two upright slabs form the west-north-west wall and a partially collapsed slab encloses the chamber to the north-north-east. There is an opening to the chamber at the east-north-east corner. Two slabs cover this chamber. At the north-north-east the monument is buried in a cairn and is heavily overgrown. Large stones fill the space between the tomb and a rock outcrop to the north-west.'

CO069-093----: The tomb is located in a narrow strip of level ground (Wth c. 8m) between two rocky ridges which are aligned E-W. The tomb faces west (270⁰) with a good view in that direction. The tomb (L c. 4.25m; Wth at W end c. 3.85m; Wth at E end c. 2.45m) is gemerally defined by two rows of side stones, by two endstones, and by four capstones. The front capstone is now lying on the ground at the front of the tomb. The middle two capstones have slipped off the inner sidestones on the north side and now rest at an askew angle largely blocking access to the chamber area. The rearmost capstone is also lying on the ground. There is some access to the interior at the western end beneath the leaning capstones. Parallel with the front sidestone and c. 0.35m inside it and 09m back from its front edge, is a single upright stone (0.5m x 0.1m; H 0.3m) on which rests a subsidary capstone. The visible area of the interior is strawn with loose stones. There are four inner sidestones on the north side and three outer ones, the two lines set c. 0.5m apart. The tallest and largest upright stone now evident is the front (W) outer sidestone on the north side (H 1.15m; L 1.15m; Wth 0.25m). There is a further upright stone in line with the endstones which is slightly outside the line of the inner stones. The sidestones on the south side are not as well preserve, but appear to be four inside and outside; the eastern-most stone on the inside line is fallen as are the second and fourth stone from the front on the outside line. The two parallel endstones are set c. 2m apart. The inner stone is the larger of the two.

CO070-035----:
In flat pasture, c. 300m NW of the confluence of the Foherish and Sullane Rivers, and c. 250m NE of Carigaphooca tower house (CO070-034----). Carrigaphooca means ‘stone of the púca’ (ghost or fairy).Three stones survive indicating a stone circle of a diameter of at least 5.5m, however, it is difficult to determine how many stones originally formed the perimeter of the circle. Windele and Conlon mention five stones, four still standing and one lying down (Ó Nualláin 1984a, 15; Conlon 1918, 139). It was described as early as the 18th century as ‘the remains of a druid altar, encompassed with a circle of stones, pitched endways’ (Smith 1750, vol. 1, 182). Based on the evidence Ó Nualláin (Ibid) suggests the circle may have been comprised of seven orthostats, and an internal quartz stone. The tallest stone is to the S of the circle, and it is oriented SSE-NNW (H 2.2m max, Wth 1m max, T 0.2 to 0.4m). Directly facing it to the N is the shortest stone, with the same orientation (H and Wth: 1.1m, T 0.37 to 0.55m). The third standing stone is to the E, and oriented E-W (H 0.85m, Wth 1m max, T 0.2 to 0.3m). Directly to the W of the tallest stone is a reclining stone which was likely part of the circle (L c. 1.2m, Wth c. 0.7m, T c. 0.5-0.6m at the base). There are also at least one other reclining stone that may have part of the monument, though it is not possible to say for certain; it is located within the circle, to the W of the E stone (H 0.7m, L 1.15m, T 0.22m). (O Nualláin 1984a, 15, no. 11)
This is a National Monument in State Ownership (no. 255).
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 3: Mid Cork' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

Comprises well-preserved wedge-shaped gallery (L3.8m; Wth c. 1.2m at W, 0.35m at E end) aligned ESE-WNW, represented by four sidestones to N and S, and backstone outside gallery walls at E end; surrounded by closely set outer walling. Two overlapping roofstones cover gallery. Gallery decreases in height from W to E. No indications of surrounding mound. Wedge-tomb (CO080-009----) stands 150m to SSE. According to Finlay (1973, 168), six cup marks on one roofstone and five on other. (de Valera and O Nualláin 1982, 18, Co. 24)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 3: Mid Cork' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

In undulating hilly terrain, in an area of felled coniferous forestry. This wedge tomb is situated 20m N of a large expanse of outcropping rock. The remains comprise a gallery (L 2.73m; Wth 1.05m at W, narrowing to 0.95m at E), aligned WSW-ENE, represented by two sidestones at N, three to the S, and a single backstone at E. Two longitudinally set jambstones stand inside the W end. The gallery is surrounded by outer-walling, two stones to the N, one to the E, and four along the S side. A partially exposed prostrate slab (1.35m x 0.8m) lying immediately outside the S outer-walling may be a displaced roofstone. A second slab (L 1m; Wth 0.47m) lies in the gallery area.
The above description is derived from 'The Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 5' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009).

CO083-112001-:
On level tract of ground in valley headwaters of Brouen River, a tributary of River Bride. Comprises long gallery (L 4.4m; Wth 1.95m at W, 0.95m at E end) aligned E-W, represented by six sidestones to N, four to S and backstone outside gallery walls at E end. Two jamb-like pillar stones stand at W end of gallery; prostrate slab between them may be displaced closing stone. Closely set outer walling survives along N and S sides. Gallery decreases in height from W to E; large stone on end in E part and another displaced stone at W end may be roofstones. Slight traces of mound survive to W and S. Large block (CO083-112002-) stands c. 10m to S. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1982, 22-3, Co. 32)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 3: Mid Cork' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload/revision: 14 January 2009

CO090-021001-:
This is the most southerly of two wedge tombs situated on a gently sloping terrace in blanket bog at the head of the Canrooska River valley on the upper slopes of Barraboy Mountain; there are fine views from the monument to the S, overlooking Glengarriff Harbour and Bantry Bay. The remains comprise a gallery (L 3.2m; Wth 1.25m at W, narrowing to c. 0.75m at E), aligned NE-SW, largely enveloped in peat. The N side is formed by at least three stones and the tops of two others are exposed on the S side; the E end is closed by a backstone. The W end is sealed by a substantial septal-stone inset in the gallery sides and is fronted by a portico formed by single orthostats on each side with two further jamb-like stones set inside them. The E section of the chamber is flanked by three close-set outer-wall stones along the N and S sides. An inclined slab protruding from the peat immediately W of the portico may represent some other element of closure at this end or it could delimit the W end of the outer-walling. The gallery is covered by two partially displaced roofstones (W slab: 2.2m x 1.45m; T c. 0.12m; E slab: 1.8m x 2.3m; Wth c. 0.15m). The second wedge tomb (CO090-021002-) is 20m to the N.
The above description is derived from 'The Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 5' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009).
Date of upload: 22 December 2009
CO090-021002-:

It consists of a gallery (L c. 3.4m; Wth 1.35 at W, narrowing to c. 0.85m at E), aligned ENE-WSW, largely enveloped in peat. The N side is formed by four stones and three are visible along the S side; the E end is closed by an inset backstone. The W end is partially closed by a transversely set septal-like slab abutting the W stone of the S side; this leaves an entrance gap of 0.5m. A single, close-set outer-wall stone is exposed along the N side. The gallery is covered by three partially displaced roofstones. The W stone (2.6m x 1.6m; T 0.15-0.2m) partially overlaps the second (1.5m x 1.4m; T 0.2m). The third (1.7m x 0.8m; T c. 0.15m) covers the E end of the gallery. The second wedge tomb (CO090-021001-) is 20m to the S and there is a standing stone (CO090-034----) c. 200m to the NW.

CO091-010007-:
On a dry grassy upland terrace, on the W side of the upper reaches of the Barony River valley with fine views to the SE and S along the valley to Glengarriff Harbour. The remains consist of a well-preserved gallery (L 4.2m; Wth 1.1m at W, narrowing only slightly to 0.95m at E), aligned NNE-SSW. In the following description the monument is described as if aligned E-W. The N and S sides are each formed by three stones and an inset backstone closes the E end. The entrance stones at the W end are exceptionally tall (S stone: H 1.75m; N stone: H 1.15m). A low, longitudinally set, jamb-like stone (H 0.35m) stands immediately S of the N entrance stone. The sides are neatly framed by close-set outer-walling, four stones to N and S. The chamber area appears to have been dug out and according to local tradition, the monument had been investigated in the early twentieth century in a search for 'treasure'. One roofstone (L 1.5m: Wth 1.2m; T > 0.1m) lies immediately W of the entrance and a second (L 2.5m; Wth 1.5m; T 0.15m) rests at an angle against a S sidestone at the E end of the gallery. Traces of a mound are evident curving about the E end of the gallery. There are a number of hut sites in the vicinity (CO090-010004- c. 60m to the NW and CO090-010010-; CO090-010003-; CO090-010005-; CO090-010011-; CO090-010002- located 200m; 230m; 250m; 260m and c. 300m to the SW, respectively). There is a standing stone (CO090-010009-) 200m to the SSW and enclosures (CO090-010008-; CO090-010006-) c. 100m and 188m to the SE and SW, respectively. Two other wedge tombs (CO091-013----; CO091-014003-) are across the valley c. 1.4km to the SE.
The above description is derived from 'The Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 5' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009).
Date of upload: 22 December 2009

CO091-013----:
Within a coniferous forest (planted 1991) on the W-facing slope of the upper reaches of the Barony River valley with views to the SE and S along the valley to Glengarriff Harbour. The remains consist of a collapsed gallery (L 2.6m; Wth c. 1.1m), aligned E-W. The N and S sides are each formed by single thin slabs which have fallen inwards and their tops rest against each other; the E end is closed by a backstone. Two transversely set, jamb-like stones front the W end of the gallery leaving an entrance gap of 0.55m. Immediately W of the S jamb are two uprights which, together with a corresponding almost prostrate slab to the N, indicate a portico arrangement at this end (L 1.1m). The gallery was covered by two roofstones. The first (1.3m x 0.95m; T 0.1-0.15m) lies immediately E of the S jamb and partially overlaps the second (2.65m x > 1.5m; T 0.12-0.15m) which covers the remainder of the gallery. Another wedge tomb (CO091-014003-) is located c. 900m to the SW and a third (CO091-010007-) is visible across the valley 1.4km to the WNW.
The above description is derived from 'The Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 5' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009).
Date of upload: 22 December 2009
CO091-014003-:
Within a coniferous forest (planted 1991) on the W-facing slope of the upper reaches of the Barony River valley with views to the SE and S along the valley to Glengarriff Harbour. The remains consist of a gallery (L 3.7m; Wth 0.8m), aligned E-W, divided into two almost equal chambers by a transversely set slab placed about midway along its length. The E chamber (L. 1.7m) is represented by a backstone and a thin slab which formed the E component of the S side; there is no surviving N side. The W chamber (L 1.7m) is open to the W and has single sidestones to the N and S. An almost recumbent slab, set transversely c. 1.2m in front of the W of this chamber, may be interpreted as a possible septal-stone. A number of overlapping, inclined and prostrate slabs immediately S of the gallery might represent outer-walling. The W chamber is almost completely covered by a roofstone (2m x 1.2m; T 0.15m) and a second roofstone lies in the E chamber (1.4m x at least 1.2m exposed; T 0.2m). There is a substantial stone (L 1.85m x 0.40m; H 0.85m) standing upright c. 4m N of the tomb; its relationship to the monument is unclear. An enclosure (CO091-014002-) is located 62m to the N and there are remains of pre-bog walls (CO091-014001-) 140m to the NE. Another wedge tomb (CO091-013----) is located c. 900m to the NE and a third (CO091-010007-) is visible across the valley 1.3km to the NW.
The above description is derived from 'The Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 5' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009).
Date of upload: 22 December 2009

CO092-019----:
Prominently situated on bog-covered hillock on NW slopes of Knockbreteen. This row of five stones, aligned NE-SW, is 5.8m in overall length. It was excavated in 1977 (Lynch 1981, 69-74). The NE stone is 0.4m L, 0.25m T and 0.5m H. The next stone, 0.5m to SW, is 0.8m L, 0.3m T and 1.3m H. The third stone, 1.05m further to the SW, leans to the SW; it is 0.3m L, 0.45m T and 1.05m H. A fragment, 1.3m by 0.5m by 0.3m, has been split from this stone and lies beside it at the NE. The fourth stone, 0.9m from the third, is 0.5m L, 0.3m T and 0.95m H. Beside this is a prostrate slab, 3.5m in maximum dimension. The SW stone, 0.25m from the last, is 1.1m L, 0.35m T and 1.05m H. The only find recovered from the excavation was a thumb-shaped flint scraper. Charcoal from the basal peat overlying the site gave a C14 determination of 3265 ± 55 bp (GrN-9281). (Ó Nualláin 1988, 234, no. 33; Roberts 1988, Ch. 5, no. 29).

In rough grazing, close to the foot of a W-facing slope in a clearing within a coniferous plantation at the head of Sruhaunphadeen valley on the NE side of Douce Mountain. The wedge-shaped gallery (L 1.95m; Wth 1.12m at W, narrowing to 0.65m at E), aligned WNW-ESE, is closed by a double backstone (H 0.45m) at E. Both the N and S sides are each formed by two uprights with the larger of the two set at the W end; the W end of the S side is broken and appears to represent a detached third stone. Three close-set outer-wall stones flank the N side of the gallery and a single outer-wall stone stands outside the E end of the S side. The E end of the gallery is covered by a roofstone (1.5m x 1m: T 0.15m), sloping to the E. Several portions of a broken slab lie prostrate among the ferns immediately to the W of the entrance and may represent the remnants of the roofstone from the W half of the gallery. Another wedge-tomb (CO093-001----) is c. 150m to the NNE.
The above description is derived from 'The Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 5' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009).
Date of upload: 22 December 2009

The roofstone is similar in many respects to those used to cover boulder-burials but the support-stones are more typical of a megalithic tomb. The local name for the tomb is 'altar'. On level bog-covered shoulder, on NW-facing slope of W end of Maughanaclea Hills. Excavated in 1938 (O Ríordáin 1939, 46-49). Circle complete; stones are 0.7m to 1.65m L, 0.25m to 0.45m T and 0.65m to 1.2m H. Internal measurement along main axis, aligned NE-SW, is 2.8m. Excavation showed that stones were not deeply sunk in ground, but were packed at base with small stones. Two shallow trenches intersecting at right angles, filled with dark humified soil, were found within circle, and interpreted as trenches for crossed wooden sleepers which may have held an upright. On the SW-facing slopes of the Maughanaclea Hills in an area of boggy upland. The tomb is located in a hollow between two natural rises to the W and E and is incorporated in the townland boundary separating Ardrah from Gortnacowley. Two overlapping slabs (H 1.2m), aligned ENE-WSW, lean slightly to the S and represent the S side of the gallery (L 2.8m) which, together with the backstone, appear to be the only stones in their original positions. The stones forming the N gallery side were displaced when a drain was dug along this side of the boundary c. 30 years ago (local info.). Two prostrate slabs lying in the gallery area W of the backstone probably represent the remains of the N side. A prostrate slab (2.1m x 1.5m; T 0.15m) lying c. 1m to the SE of the tomb is probaby the displaced roofstone. Outside the SW corner of the gallery, a slab leaning to the E may be a displaced façade stone; a second stone, with its W end stuck in the ground, leans against the former. A slab (2.1m x 0.5m; T 0.2m) lying in the bottom of the drain 4m W of the tomb may be a displaced part of the structure. A cairn (CO106-085---) is located 190m to the SW.
The above description is derived from 'The Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 5' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009).
Date of upload: 22 December 2009

CO107-025----:
On level platform on steep NW-facing slope of narrow valley of Clodagh river. Row of three stones, aligned NE-SW, and 8.9m in overall length. NE stone is 0.9m L, 0.65m T and 1.2m H. Next and tallest stone, 2m to the SW, is 1.4m L, 0.8m T and 1.8m H. SW stone, 3.2m from last, is 1.25m L, 1.35m T and 1.7m H. OS 6-inch map (1842) depicts fourth stone to W of middle stone: this stone is not now present. Basal peat from test pit dug c. 5m N of row yielded a radiocarbon determination of 975 ± 45 bp (GrN-9282) (Lynch 1981, 111-3; O Nualláin 1988, 236, no. 42; Roberts 1988, Ch. 5, no. 41).

Within a mature coniferous wood, to the W of Coolkellure Lake. A row of six stones, aligned NE-SW, measures 5.5m in overall length. The NE stone (0.4m x 0.4m; H 0.46m) is situated 0.6m from the second stone (1.08m x 0.44m; H 1.07m) at the SW. The third stone (0.66m x 0.35m; H 0.78m) is located 0.2m to the SW. The fourth stone (0.21m x 0.25m; H 0.66m) stands 0.15m to the SW of the third stone. The fifth stone (0.45m x 0.15m; H 0.8m) is 0.25m to the SW of the previous stone. The sixth stone (0.8m x 0.6m; H 1.05) is 0.7m to the SW of the fifth stone. All stones are largely covered with moss and are surrounded by forest debris. Smaller quartz stones have been placed on top of the second and third stones.
The above description is derived from 'The Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 5' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009).

CO115-094----:
In rough pasture, with outcropping rock on the bog-covered SW-facing slopes overlooking Castletownbere and Berehaven Harbour. The lower portion of the outer element of the tomb is enveloped in peat. The wedge-shaped gallery (L 1.6m; Wth 0.72m at E end), aligned ENE-WSW, is closed at E by a backstone. The N side is represented by a single slab and the S side is formed by two uprights; the W of these leans markedly inwards. The gallery is partly covered by a roofstone (1.85m x 1.75m; T 0.15-0.2m) which has slipped forward over the collapsed S sidestone and slopes down to the SW blocking the W end of the monument. An inclined slab set immediately outside the S side near the backstone may be part of outer-walling. A standing stone (CO115-095----) is located 140m to the NE and a fulacht fia (CO115-096----) 180m to the SE.
The above description is derived from 'The Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 5' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009).

The N side is formed by a single slab and the S by three inward leaning slabs (overall L 2.75m); the two W stones overlap. CO119-128----:
This monument was reported to the Archaeological Survey of Ireland by Tony Miller on 4 September 2013. He describes it as follows:
"A five stone row sited on a level area near the top of a west facing slope, overlooking the  River Ilen.  In an area of improved pasture dominated by a drumlin swarm, immediately south of the castle at Castledonovan. The row is in the north east corner of a field with a farm track passing close to the north and east. There is now access into the field as it is on one of the new walking trails created in and around Drimoleague. The landowners, Emma and Marcus, run an Alpaca farm and educational centre.
 The stone row has an overall length of 3.9m and consists of five stones with the tallest in the middle.  The alignment of the row is north east – south west (30°- 210°) and all the stones are of a similar size and shape with only the central one being taller. The measurements of the stones are, from the south west-
1.	0.8m H; 0.44m W; 0.12m Th. 0.5m from
2.	0.89m H; 0.43m W 0.17m Th. 0.38m from
3.	1.5m H; 0.54m W;0.17m Th. 0.47m from
4.	0.87m H; 0.41m W; 0.2m Th. 0.001m from
5.	0.88H; 0.55m W; 0.11m Th.
Approximately 3m to the west of the alignment is a line of large slabs of rock lying flat on the ground or on each other forming a raised boundary to this corner of the field. The boundary makes a short return for a few meters along the south west end of the alignment. To the north east it continues on into a thicket of fuschia and briars. This boundary covers some exposed bedrock so it could have been a convenient place to dump field clearance or it could have been an attempt to demarcate this part of the field containing the stone row."
Compiled by: Denis Power
Date of upload: 16 September 2013

Only the W section of the gallery is exposed together with a single endstone (either a backstone or kerb) at the E of the monument. The total length of the monument to the endstone is 4.4m. Exposed stones indicate a gallery length of at least 2.3m. The gallery (Wth 1.07m at W, narrowing to 0.77m at the estimated centre) is aligned WSW-ENE and the W section is represented on each side by two sidestones and three outer-wall stones; the stones decrease in height from W to E. The W two outer-wall stones flanking the entrance are higher than their corresponding gallery sidestones. Cutway bog to the E of the monument is partly responsible for exposing the E endstone.

Situated in an area of outcropping rock with dense furze and brambles, overlooking Dunmanus Bay to the S. The monument was cleared of vegetation on rediscovery in 1995 (see Power et al. 1992, 43). The circle is incomplete: four erect and seven prostrate slabs indicate a circle of eleven stones. Both entrance stones and the axial stone are prostrate and the sockets for three fallen stones are visible with some packing-stones still in situ. Orthostats are 0.9m to 1.4m L, 0.2m to 0.55m T and 0.8m to 1.4m H. The internal measurement along the main axis, aligned NE-SW, is c. 7.5m. Two shallow pits were dug within the circle in modern times, one at the centre and the other beside an orthostat to S. The cover-stone of a possible boulder-burial (CO130-016001-) stands in the NW quadrant of the circle and a second example (CO130-043----) stands immediately outside the circle to S.
The above description is derived from 'The Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 5' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009).

On broad shelf of pasture near foot of Mount Gabriel. Monuments excavated in 1988 by Dr. W.F. O'Brien. Large rounded boulder (1.8m x 1.6m; T 1.15m) to E, rests above three support stones. Excavation revealed central pit containing charcoal fragments which provided a C14 determination of 3080 ±35 B.P. (GrN-15716). Seven narrow stake-holes surround monument. No human bone or artefacts were recovered in primary association with monument. Second boulder burial (CO139-037002-) 3.8m to E; sub-rectangular cover stone (1.5m x 0.95m;T c. 0.75m) supported at N by three stones. Support stones placed on top of large backfilled pit. No burial evidence or artifacts recovered. (pers.comm. Dr. W.F. O'Brien)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 1: West Cork' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1992). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload/revision: 14 January 2009

CO140-060----:
In rough pasture between two knolls of outcropping rock with occasional rock and boulders protruding from the surface. There are views to the S and SW over undulating pasture to the mouth of Roaringwater Bay. The monument, incorporated in a stone field wall, consists of a gallery (L 2.m; Wth 0.65m at the open NE end), aligned NE-SW. The W end of the monument has collapsed and is obsured by the roofstone and field-clearance material. The S side forms part of the field wall and is represented by three stones that rise in height to the W. Only the E stone of the N side survives and there is no evidence for a backstone. The roofstone (2.2m x at least 1m; T 0.2m) rests on the two opposing sidestones forming the E end of the gallery and slopes downwards to the entrance area where it is covered by field-clearance material. The monument appears to have collapsed in antiquity as there is a layer of peat on top of the roofstone below the field-clearance material.
The above description is derived from 'The Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 5' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009).
Date of upload: 22 December 2009

CO143-051002-:
In pasture on a natural rock terrace on the S slope of a low hill. This stone circle was excavated in 1957 (Fahy 1959, 1-27), and the nearby fulacht fiadh (CO143-051002-) and hut site (CO143-051001-) in 1958 (Fahy 1960, 1-17). The circle consisted of seventeen stones; two are missing and one has fallen. The stones are 0.55m to 2.05m L, 0.2m to 0.65m T and 1.1m to 2.05m H. On the upper surface of the axial stone, which is the largest stone in the circle, are two shallow cup-marks, one surrounded by an oval carving. The internal measurement along the main axis, aligned NE-SW, is 9m. Five pits were found within the circle, sealed beneath compacted gravel floor; one pit contained the deposit of cremated human bone, fragments of shale and numerous sherds of coarse fabric pot. Initial radiocarbon dating of the charcoal from the burial returned as BC 13 ± 140 (Fahy 1960, 17), which was later amended to AD 600 ± 120 (D-62) which is 'clearly anomalous' (O Nualláin 1984a, 10). However, a more recent analysis of the charcoal from the grave returned a date range of 1124-794 BC (Waddell 1998, 169), making it a lot older than first thought. Other finds from the circle included seven pieces of flint, including a small convex scraper. (O Nualláin 1984a, 24. no. 37; Roberts 1988, Ch. 2, no. 5)
This is a National Monument in State Guardianship (no. 381).
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 1: West Cork' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1992). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

CO148-001----:
This monument was excavated over a five-week period, in June-July 1990 and was followed by restoration of the megalithic chamber in September 1990 (O'Brien 1999, 141-89). The chamber originally consisted of two sub-parallel orthostat rows oriented approximately NE-SW (249-069 degrees). The N row contained three contiguous sidestones and the southern row had two certain sidestones separated by a gap of 0.85m: this probably contained a third upright slab. These were set in foundation trenches and formed a chamber or gallery measuring 4.25m in length. The chamber decreases in height from 1.26m at the W entrance to 0.90m at the E end. The ground plan is similarly wedge-shaped, ranging from 1.88m wide at the SW to 1.20m at the NE end which was closed by a backstone slab. No evidence of a closing slab or septal arrangement was found in the course of the excavationsa at the open W end of the monument. The chamber probably was roofed originally by two overlapping roofstones, only one of which survived. No evidence was recovered to suggest that it had been covered by a cairn or mound. A bronze axe dating to the Early Bronze Age and two pieces of raw copper were found as a single deposit on the N side of the tomb entrance. No other prehistoric artefacts were recovered and there was no evidence of burials. Radio-carbon determinations indicate that the monument was constructed during the later stages of the Early Bronze Age, c. 1700-1500 BC, and had witnessed intermittent activity in the later prehistoric and historic periods. (Power et al. 1992, 19, no. 40)

CO148-005----:
On a roadside platform, c. 30m from and 4m above the rocky shoreline of the NE edge of Toormore Bay. This wedge tomb was excavated in 1989 by Dr. William F. O'Brien (see summary: https://excavations.ie/report/1989/Cork/0000842/). It consists of a simple slab-built chamber aligned ENE-WSW. This gallery is formed by two orthostat rows of three slabs each (L 3.4m; Wth 1.9m at W end, 1m at E end). One roofstone remained in position above the E end; a second rested against the W end of the gallery. No clear evidence for a cairn was recovered during excavation, which may be explained by intensive post-medieval cultivation and the early 19th-century road construction. The socket for a backstone and a low stone kerb feature at the entrance were uncovered. The latter contained three fragments of cetacean bone deliberately deposited in this construction context, and overlaid two pits on either side of the entrance which contained shattered slaty stone, possibly tooling debris gathered after the deliberate shaping of the orthostats and capstones. Two cobble-hammers used in this activity were also recovered.
A pit containing votive deposits of limpet, periwinkle shells and fish bones was found at the E end of the chamber, and a small spread of cremated human bone was uncovered inside the entrance area. Finds outside the chamber included struck pebble flint, including two end-scrapers and a broken hollow scraper, recovered in cultivation-disturbed contexts. Only a solitary fragment of struck flint was recovered from the chamber. (de Valera and O Nualláin 1982, 41, no. 61; Roberts 1988, Ch. 4, No. 19; pers. comm. Dr. W. F. O'Brien; https://excavations.ie/report/1989/Cork/0000842/)
This is a National Monument in State care (no. 645)

CO150-057----:
The tomb lies on the E side of Ringarogy Island, a small rocky eminence in the estuary of the Illen River, locally known as the Lag. Much of the island and almost all of the tomb is inundated at high tide. The tomb is covered in sea-weed and only the tops of two orthostats are visible above the high-water mark. The remains consist of a gallery (L 3m; Wth 1m), aligned ENE-WSW, formed by three sidestones to the N and three to the S. The gallery opens to the E where a transversely set, jamb-like stone (H 1.1m) standing at the E end of the N side with a further smaller orthostat (H 0.5m) to E indicates some form of elaboration of the entrance area. The W end of the gallery is closed by a substantial backstone (H 1.15m). Four prostrate slabs to the E of the entrance area and two others to the S probably represent displaced roofing elements. The mound for the most part has been removed by tidal action; three kerbstones are in situ 2m N of the gallery and three possible examples can be identified to the NW. (Shee Twohig 1995, 7-9)
The above description is derived from 'The Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 5' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009).

CO153-010----:
On summit of hill dominating N section of Clear Island. Chamber, open to NE, at centre of low cairn (diam. c. 15m). Five orthostats in line with N side of chamber, and a transversely set stone at exposed cairn edge may represent remains of passage. Stone, decorated with passage-tomb art (CO153-008---), found c. 1880 in townland of Croha West c. 1km to SW. (O'Leary 1989, 124-6) (Ó Nualláin 1989, 127).
The decorated stone (CO153-008----) and site of passage tomb (CO153-010----) from which the stone probably came from was described by O'Leary (1989, 124-6) as follows; 'In April 1984, however, an archaeological survey of Clear Island was undertaken, and on the top of the highest hill (533') in the townland of Killickaforavane, a sub-circular spread or cairn of stones was found c. 16m in diameter.  In the middle of this cairn was a small hollow bounded on three sides by orthostats.  The site consists of a sub-circular spread of boulders, slabs and stones measuring 16.5m NE by SW and 14m NW by SE. In the centre is a depression defined by five orthostats which line the SE, SW and NW sides. To the NE of this feature is a line of five orthostats running NE by SW. In line with these and at the edge of the stone.spread is an orthostat which is oriented NW by SE. There is a further single orthostat 1.5m south of the line of orthostats. Grasses and heather grow on and around the stone-spread on the little soil available and make it difficult to define the perimeter in places, especially in the west and south. There is some peat cover against south-west corner of the chamber: The orthostats vary, in height from 15cm above present ground level to 75cm above present ground level.  In the north-west quadrant there is a dry-stone pillar/ approximately 2m in height and 2.75m in diameter. This appears have been formerly used as a  trigonometrical station; a new one stands to the west of the site. Near the hilltop are stone field fences which, together with the dry-stone pillar, may have been constructed of stones from the site.  As a result of research done by Mr Éamon Lankford of the Clear Island Museum Society, we now know that the decorated stone was found about 1880, in the townland of Croha West (not in the townland of Glen as previously thought) by a Mr Ó Síocháin and Mr Ó Ríogáin while engaged in clearing a field, then the property of a Mr Shipsey.  Even without the evidence of the decorated stone, the site does suggest a megalithic monument of the Passage Tomb type. A sufficient number of orthostats remain in situ to trace a passage leading from the perimeter to the chamber in the centre of the cairn. The orientation of the passage falls well within the range of Irish passage tombs generally. The cairn diameter of c. 16m and the tomb length of 8m would place it in the small to medium examples of this type.  The field in which the decorated stone was found is a half-mile to the south-west of the hilltop, at an elevation of under 300' [91m], and is beside the roadway to South Harbour. …
